finding: The live range of $200-$825 is about right at the bottom and too low at the top. Built totals for one front CV axle, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $215-$761 (1.0-1.6 hr); midsize 2015 Accord 2.4L CVT about $198-$1,340 (1.0-1.6 hr); truck 2019 Silverado 1500 4WD about $255-$918 (1.0-2.4 hr); luxury 2015 Acura ILX 2.4L about $210-$710 (1.0-1.6 hr). The bottom: the lowest totals ($198-$255) pair a new aftermarket axle at an online price ($78-$135) with a manufacturer warranty time, so $200 is a fair floor and few real quotes will come in under it. The top: $825 covers an aftermarket axle on every class and a dealer-list axle on the Corolla and ILX 2.4L, but not the cars whose genuine shafts are expensive. Honda lists the Accord shaft at $1,084-$1,116, which builds to about $1,340, and Acura lists the ILX 2.0L shaft at $1,346-$1,432, which with 1.1 hr comes to about $1,480-$1,610. RepairPal's national average ($1,283-$1,381, with $1,075 in parts) and J.D. Power's $1,500 top figure sit in the same place. A ceiling of about $1,350 would cover a dealer-parts job on a mainstream car; $825 fits only if the range is meant to describe aftermarket parts. The spread is almost entirely parts: labor is only about $120-$385 in every class. How solid the labor times are: the low end in three classes is a Honda or Acura recall warranty time of 1.0-1.1 hr for one side, which already includes the inspection, wheel alignment and test drive; for the ILX it is the same model with the other powertrain, for the Corolla it is a Civic Hybrid and a Fit, and for the Accord the only Accord-specific figure is 1.5 hr for both sides, so its one-side low end is borrowed from the Civic Hybrid. The 1.6 hr high end in those three classes is one flat-rate figure quoted by an independent mechanic for a 2015 Subaru Forester, from a guide he does not name. The truck low end is a parts seller's 'approx 1 hour' for the Silverado itself, and its high end is GM's 2.4 hr warranty time for both sides on the same truck, used as a ceiling because no one-side time was printed; a seller quotes about 3 hours for the previous-generation truck. No class has a manufacturer one-side time for the exact example vehicle. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, J.D. Power's general statement is 1.5 to 3 hours, and a seized axle nut or a shaft rusted into the hub adds time.
extras: A quote often adds a new axle nut (usually one-time-use), an axle seal at the transmission or front differential if it is leaking or disturbed, and a top-up of transmission fluid or gear oil lost when the shaft comes out (the Honda bulletins include a fluid check). Some shops add a wheel alignment, though the manufacturer times above already include one. Shops may recommend the other side at the same time, which roughly doubles parts and adds less than double the labor (Honda allows 1.4-1.9 hr for both against 1.0-1.5 hr for one). Also possible: a refundable core charge on a remanufactured axle, the separate intermediate shaft or its bearing on cars that have one, extra labor for a seized axle nut or a shaft rusted into the wheel hub (sometimes a new wheel bearing as a result), a diagnosis or inspection fee, shop supplies and sales tax.
